comment_text:
Think of it as an outside bar. When price is moving upwards, an order block is the last up candle before a downward movement. But for it to be a valid order block, the high of that candle AND the low of that candle have to be taken by the next down candle. After this down candle, price will move down for a little while, but mark out the opening of that last up candle. When price comes back up and touches that opening price of that up candle, it will act as resistance, providing a possible entry to go short.

Same for downward price movement. Say that price is moving down, and then goes upward. The order block here would be the last down candle, before that upward movement. Remember though! This candle needs to have both its low and its high taken by the next candle, which is an up candle. Price will then move upwards, now mark the opening price of that last down candle which is the order block. When price comes back down, it may use this opening price level as support, possibly giving you a long position.

The expectancy equation explains this perfectly:
Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).

A strategy can be profitable with only a 40% win rate if the average winner is sufficiently larger than the average loser. The difficult part is surviving the losing streaks without increasing position size or abandoning the system. How do you determine when a drawdown is statistically normal versus evidence that the strategy’s edge has weakened?

comment_text:
I saw a YouTube trader draw a straight 45 degree line on a white board .  It represented the S&P 500 over its life time.
He then asked how long you intend to be investing…..eg 5 years.   So pick your starting point and go out 5 years.    Of course in between the entry point and exit point there are many up and down movements, but if you know your exit point is 5 years in the future, they don’t matter.   When you see the geometry drawn out this way it seems so simple.   
Trading and investing are two different things.   I think for the vast majority of us investing is way less dangerous.   Maybe invest 90% and trade with what’s left.  
Good luck folks.

Not financial advice only personal experience and opinion.
No problem with a Funded Futures acct. Starting with 1 micro Emini MNQ position size. When overall context and price direction is correct. Helps psychologically not to worry about the position initially. Large volume of orders or Stops get challenged by bigger players. Order flow is the game we’re playing with or against. Price always fluctuates. Not just because technical signals are causing it. But institutions can absorb volume and take in a completely different direction. 1 micro emini won’t blow your acct, even if price goes extreme in one direction before max trailing drawdown, you can always add 1 more contract and still be within risk tolerance. Of course if context changes and or change of character changes as SMC traders will notice then you can get out with less drawdown by averaging max micro positions. Maybe kind of like grid trading in crypto traders. 😮😮😮

comment_text: I've operated with this technique for a while. Problem is when you think market is uptrend, but it starts to go opposite and consistently. Once the market goes against you, you tend to increase the position, might entering on levels you think will hold, which might in fact not hold. And the more you increase the position the more is difficult to move your average price, while the market might stay for a while at much lower price... or go so down that you will have to fight with your margins (if you are able to do that!). It might require quite some time and nerves before it comes back at exit levels. On the other side, if the market goes in your favour, you will have a small position size, so smaller gains. Therefore overall, I would not advise this technique, you have to be really very careful+luck that you dont find in these situations, that when happen, are very painful. Better take a stop right away and keep operational.

comment_text:
Godinama sam promatrao ljude na Forexu kako mijenjaju indikatore, strategije i mentore i uvijek završe na istom mjestu. Jedan indikator kasni, drugi crpi signal tek nakon što je kretanje već završeno, treći izgleda savršeno na starom grafikonu, ali se raspada čim se uključi pravo tržište. Ne kažem da su svi indikatori beskorisni ili da svaki edukator namjerno obmanjuje ljude. Problem je dublji: većina početnika pokušava predvidjeti kamo će cijena ići, bez da pitaju **zašto je prije morala ići u krivom smjeru**. Tržište često prvo pokaže laž, a tek onda pokaže svoju pravu namjeru. Cijena probija prethodni maksimum i privlači kupce, uzima stop-loss cijene prodavača, a zatim se vraća. Probija dno, uvjerava ljude da počinje pad, uzima likvidnost ispod njega i naglo mijenja smjer. Ljudi to nazivaju lažnim probojem, lovom na stop-loss ili manipulacijom, ali samo ime nije dovoljno. Slijed događaja je ono što je važno. Povlačenje likvidnosti nije automatski ulazak. Zona ponude ili potražnje nije automatski ulazak. Blok naloga, FVG, linija trenda, RSI, EMA ili bilo koja strelica nije automatski unos. Prvo moram znati gdje je likvidnost. Zatim čekam da cijena uzme tu poziciju, da se zatvori natrag, promijenim kratkoročnu strukturu kroz CHoCH ili BOS i tek se onda vraćam testirati mjesto odakle je krenuo pravi impuls. Bez tog lanca događaja, gledam samo oblik na grafikonu, a ne priču iza njega. Isto vrijedi i za vremenske okvire. Jedna minuta može se činiti savršenom za kupnju, dok petnaest minuta i jedan sat i dalje vode cijenu prema nižoj likvidnosti. Manji vremenski okvir ne treba promatrati kao zasebno tržište. On je samo detalj veće slike. Azijska sesija često gradi raspon i ostavlja likvidnost iznad i ispod njega. London može zauzeti stranu, napraviti snažan prvi potez ili postaviti zamku. New York tada može potvrditi London, vratiti se na svoj račun ili potpuno preokrenuti priču. Zato sat na grafikonu, prethodni dnevni i tjedni usponi i padovi te cjenovna pozicija unutar veće zone često znače više od nove obojene strelice. Kod EUR/USD, GBP/USD i zlata, dolar čak ni ne gledam zasebno. DXY mi daje kontekst, ali nije ni ulazni nalog. Ako je dolar u ključnoj zoni i samo uzima vlastitu likvidnost, signal na drugom instrumentu može imati potpuno drugačije značenje nego što se na prvi pogled čini. Najveća zabluda nije da tržište nema pravila. Zabluda je da se ta pravila mogu svesti na jednu liniju, prijelaz dvaju prosjeka ili postotak napisan pored signala. A još veća zabluda je da će vas dobar ulaz spasiti od lošeg upravljanja rizikom. Bez jasno definirane invalidacije, pravilnog stop-lossa i kontrole veličine pozicije, čak i ispravno čitanje tržišta može se pretvoriti u gubitak. Na ovom tržištu nema nepogrešive strategije niti zajamčene dobiti. Već dugo pokušavam sve dijelove spojiti u jednu logičnu cjelinu: likvidnost, lažni proboji, sesije, viši i niži vremenski okviri, DXY, bankarske zone, promjena strukture,povratak na posljednji nalog i upravljanje rizikom. Tek tada sam shvatio da prava razlika nije u tome tko ima više indikatora, nego tko razumije **što se mora dogoditi prije nego što kvalitetan ulaz uopće smije postojati**.
Najvažniji dio te priče nisam napisao u ovom komentaru, jer bez cijelog konteksta zvuči kao još jedna brza strategija. Složio sam ga u vlastitom priručniku, bez obećanja lake zarade i bez čarobnog signala. Tko ozbiljno proučava tržište i želi razgovarati o logici iza kretanja cijene, može mi se javiti

comment_text: Swing highs, Equal highs, & Trendlines hold huge liquidity same for lows. That’s why it’s best to only enter after the they get swept. When you see equal lows below Demand, place a limit order at the equal low. If you know price wicks equal lows then you have a safe systematic entry model. If price only taps the demand imbalance but doesn’t wick the equal, lows and continues to go bullish, then delete your order and come again tomorrow. It may not wick your entry in the trade a few times before hitting your TP but when it does, you’ll have the cheapest price to sell for a huge profit.

comment_text: You won’t. 😂. You’ll make no profit for a good 2 years. Could even be 3. To really master this game, you need to master yourself so your discipline and psychology. Waste of time. You need to feel the real markets in real time. It will teach you patience and quick decision making. Creating your strategy is easy once you know the basics, but creating a system and following your rules and risk management and demo forward testing it for a whole year while documenting every trade is the hard part. But it’s all worth it because the basics strategy you first practiced will slowly unwind itself into a big complex system that only you understand through out your Practice year on demo then it will all click toward the middle or end of the year. It will all make sense. The simple strategy you first practiced will be your own personal system that you’ve created from adding on new confluences, from new information you’ve learned and experienced while trading. Believe me bro. That’s the only way to really be profitable. Then when you’ve got a whole years data showing you that you’re profitable, then you do it again on a live account for a year trading your finalised system sticking to your rules strictly. The live trading year is mainly a focus on your psychology and how you handle wins and losses trading your real money. If you ended that year sticking to your rules and profitable, that’s when you can get funded because you’ve proved to yourself you’re profitable. Don’t go live as a beginner looking to get funded. Believe me bro, in your first year as a beginner, you ain’t learned nothing yet😂😂. Experience will teach you what you need to know. Take your journey slow and steady. It’s not a race but a marathon. RETESTING THE EXTREME ZONE & THE LOGIC BEHIND BANK MOVEMENTS

The market didn’t revisit the extreme zone by accident—it returned to close a banking order that was positioned around the 50% mark of a wick. On the lower timeframes, we can spot liquidity within the wick, but on the higher timeframes, like the Daily, the story becomes clearer: the market shifted direction and formed a new Higher High (HH).

Here's the key: the market always pulls back to the last order that pushed it forward—the one that caused the recent HH or LL—before continuing the move. That’s why we must analyze higher timeframes first and then fine-tune entries on lower ones. Only when we combine both can we see the true narrative unfold.

Smaller timeframes always follow the structure of the higher ones. Banks move capital, revisit their positions to reinvest, and then drive the market where they want it to go. Our job is not to predict—it’s to respond to their inevitable reactions, once we truly understand how the market breathes.

Meanwhile, banks continuously bait retail traders, luring them into traps to collect the liquidity they need for their next move—one that’s often already telegraphed on the higher timeframes.

So what do we do?

We study. We stay present. We train our eyes. We learn to read what the banks are saying—without saying it. Because banks don’t speak with headlines—they speak through the chart, and with each candle, they negotiate.

Final word:
Follow the money—not the noise. Play their game—but play it against them.
